claims.text: An actively learned machine-learning interatomic potential can be iteratively trained through training, exploration, and ab initio labeling stages using crystalline and liquid configurations.
The proposed method is applicable to refractory multicomponent alloys such as Mo–Nb–Ti and Mo–Nb–Ti–Ta in both crystalline and liquid states.
The relevant temperature range is near melting, typically at or above approximately 0.9Tm.
The liquid state of refractory high-entropy alloys near melting exhibits significant configurational variability.

Local-environment descriptors such as atom-centered symmetry functions or smooth overlap of atomic positions can represent many-body interactions and chemical disorder in both solid and liquid phases.
Active learning and continuous enrichment of the training set will represent the high-dimensional liquid configurational space more accurately than semi-empirical EAM models.
A more accurate representation of solid and liquid configurations will improve phase-space overlap between the machine-learning reference and the ab initio target.
Improved reference–target phase-space overlap will reduce thermodynamic-integration path mismatch.
TOR-TILD's EAM references struggle to represent the broad range of configurations in an ab initio liquid.
The proposed potential is expected to reduce TI path mismatch by at least a factor of approximately two relative to TOR-TILD's EAM references.
An order-of-magnitude reduction in TI path mismatch may be achievable.
Free-energy estimates from the actively learned potential should agree with full ab initio benchmarks to within approximately 10% deviation.
Machine-learning potentials have been used for calculations in a refractory Nb–Mo–Ta concentrated alloy.
Accuracy may degrade for compositions or temperatures significantly outside the active-learning training domain.
Unforeseen ordering phenomena absent from the training data may reduce the improvement obtained from the machine-learning reference.

The proposed test compares otherwise parallel thermodynamic-integration calculations using an EAM reference and an actively learned machine-learning reference against full ab initio free-energy benchmarks.
Failure to obtain a factor-of-two reduction in TI path mismatch, or a free-energy deviation exceeding approximately 10% from the ab initio benchmark, is defined as falsification.
